In Lorenz-96 \citep{lorenz1995predictability,lorenz2006predictability} with a known law and an unknown forcing, observed with noise for 0.84~LT, we sample the Bayesian posterior over state and forcing for each of 200 independent instances. Immediately after the observation window the two signs are confident about equally often (98.3\% of intervention-sign questions against 97.0\% of forecast signs at lead 0; 91.4\% against 92.0\% at 1~LT). From 1.5~LT the intervention sign falls behind: 72.4\% against 85.0\% at 2~LT, 40.4\% against 67.0\% at 3~LT, and 14.25\% against 39.0\% at 4~LT. Of the confident intervention-sign answers at 2~LT, 16.1\% are given by climatology at the true forcing. These all come from the uniform forcing decrease, whose sign the attractor supplies up to 2~LT. For the other seven patterns the climatological ensemble gives either sign with probability between 0.50 and 0.56 at every lead, so every confident answer about them comes from the observations. The pre-specified same-lead difference between the observation-confident $S$ share and the confident $F_c$ share is $-0.243$ at 2~LT (99\% interval $[-0.352, -0.136]$) and $-0.266$ at 3~LT ($[-0.388, -0.152]$); both meet the criterion. Pairwise orderings are confident for 74.0\% of pairs at 2~LT and 43.3\% at 3~LT, and the best action is confident for 65.0\% and 20.5\% of instances. The development panel gave the same pattern: $-0.221$ ($[-0.322, -0.106]$) at 2~LT.

old_text: A natural objection is that the result reflects only the small size of the interventions. We re-forecast the saved development posterior draws at five amplitudes, 0.04, 0.08, 0.16, 0.32 and 0.64 (0.5\% to 8\% of the forcing), with the climatological ensemble re-run at each amplitude. No new sampling was done, and realized-outcome calibration was not recomputed at the changed amplitudes, so these are exploratory readings (Table~\ref{tab:amplitude}, Figure~\ref{fig:amplitude}). From 0.04 to 0.16 the confident intervention-sign share at 2~LT is essentially unchanged (73.8\%, 73.5\%, 74.4\%), as is the paired loss difference ($-0.228$, $-0.220$, $-0.210$, each with a 99\% interval below zero). At 0.32 and 0.64 the share rises, most at longer leads (at 4~LT from 18.0\% at 0.16 to 32.6\% at 0.64). Climate-confident answers appear at 2.5~LT (and at 3~LT for 0.64), and the paired ordering is no longer detected (0.64: $-0.101$, $[-0.252, 0.088]$). At every amplitude the confident intervention-sign share at 2 and 3~LT stays below the forecast sign's.

old_text: \paragraph{A perturbed-last-frame ensemble.} The 128-member ensemble formed by perturbing the last observed frame with the observation noise, with the forcing estimated from the observations, is a common way to start an ensemble from a short window. At 2~LT it is confident on 38.8\% of intervention signs, against the posterior's 72.4\%, and its confident observation-dependent answers are right 98.5\% of the time (lower bound 95.3\%). It is reliable but answers less; Cohen's $\kappa$ with the posterior's classifications is 0.48.
new_text: \paragraph{A perturbed-last-frame ensemble.} We form a 128-member ensemble by perturbing the last observed frame with the observation noise and using the forcing estimated from the observations by a one-dimensional fit. At 2~LT it is confident on 38.8\% of intervention signs, against the posterior's 72.4\%, and its confident observation-dependent answers are right 98.5\% of the time (lower bound 95.3\%). It is reliable but answers less; Cohen's $\kappa$ with the posterior's classifications is 0.48.

old_text: If an intervention's effect has its own horizon, measurements chosen for the forecast need not be the ones that resolve it. In the first 60 confirmation instances (by index) in which the comparison between the two interventions with the lowest posterior-mean cost was not confident at 2~LT, we added four precise point measurements of the state at time zero, with noise one tenth of the observation noise. The sites were chosen by one of four rules: (Q) greedily reducing the posterior variance of the decision difference, as in ensemble-sensitivity targeting \citep{xie2013observing}; (F) the same rule for the unforced forecast; (V) largest posterior variance of the state, the family \citet{lorenz1998optimal} found best for forecast error; and (R) random sites. We then resampled the posterior (Table~\ref{tab:measure}). No arm produced a confident wrong answer. On the development panel, question-targeted measurement resolved 27 of 60 decisions against at most 13, with every McNemar $p < 0.001$. On the confirmation panel it resolved 15 against 10, 7 and 4. Against random sites it met the frozen 1\% level ($p = 0.004$); against spread-targeted sites it narrowly missed it ($p = 0.011$), and against forecast-targeted sites it did not reach it ($p = 0.0625$). The frozen criterion required a margin of 0.10 and $p \le 0.01$ against all three, so the advantage did not confirm.

Arm Q settled 15 (lower bound 0.82, coverage 91.7\%), so the margin, the paired tests and the count all fell short, and the advantage did not confirm.

old_text: \paragraph{Two signs, two kinds of knowledge.} The forecast sign asks on which side of the climatological mean the posterior's window energies lie. The intervention sign asks whether the posterior's draws agree on the sign of a small difference, which each draw computes along its own trajectory. The intervention's displacement of the state grows with the same instability that spreads the posterior: the ratio of the two is nearly constant after 1~LT. We read the loss as a failure of agreement on how that displacement projects onto the cost; the projection itself was not measured. Shared uncertainty helps at first, and helps a great deal (the median $z_D$ is 3.6 times the median $z_F$ at lead 0), but the difference inherits the decorrelation of the draws at a rate the forecast anomaly does not. A correlation of 0.975 sounds like near-complete cancellation. It still leaves 3\% of the summed variance in the difference, and at the effect sizes of a 2\% forcing change that is enough to leave 28\% of intervention signs below 95\% confidence at 2~LT, against 15\% of forecast signs.

\paragraph{Why amplitude does not help, until it does.} For a small amplitude $a$, $D_k \approx a\, g_k(x_0, F)$, where $g_k$ is the instance's linear response. Both the posterior mean and the posterior standard deviation of $D_k$ then scale with $a$, so $z_D$, and with it the confidence horizon of the sign, does not depend on how large the intervention is. The development readings agree: from 0.5\% to 2\% of the forcing the confident share and the loss ordering barely move. Within that range, making the intervention larger makes its effect larger, not more knowable. Only at 4--8\% of the forcing does the share rise, and there climate-confident answers appear at longer leads. In Lorenz's terms, a small intervention's effect is a question of predictability of the first kind and inherits the instability that limits the trajectory. A large one begins to acquire the forced, attractor-level response of the second kind \citep{lorenz1975climatic}, which fluctuation--dissipation theory describes \citep{leith1975climate,majda2010high}. We read the amplitude results as consistent with this picture; they are development readings without realized calibration at the changed amplitudes.

old_text: For one observed instance of a chaotic system, the posterior can say how far ahead each question about it can be answered, and the answer differs by question. The sign of a small intervention's effect is confident about as often as the forecast sign just after the observations, and less often from 1.5~LT. In paired comparisons its confidence is lost first more often than not, despite factual and counterfactual futures that share almost all their uncertainty. In this setting, then, the forecast horizon is not the intervention horizon, and a model used to act would need to report the second.
new_text: For one observed instance of a chaotic system, the posterior can say how far ahead each question about it can be answered, and the answer differs by question. Just after the observations the sign of a small intervention's effect is confident for 98\% of questions and the forecast sign for 97\%; at 2 and 3~LT the observation-dependent intervention-sign share is lower by about a quarter of the questions. In paired comparisons its confidence is lost first more often than not, despite factual and counterfactual futures that share almost all their uncertainty. In this setting, then, the forecast horizon is not the intervention horizon, and a model used to act would need to report the second.
